preamble: Total progressive assimilation of the alveolar nasal [n] to a preceding velar stop, turning the cluster /gn/ into a geminate [gg]. The classic case is Middle Indo-Aryan, where nasals assimilate to a preceding stop: Sanskrit agni 'fire' and nagna 'naked' became Pali aggi and nagga, and the same outcome appears in Ashokan Prakrit agi /aggi/ and Prakrit ṇagga. The nasal loses its nasality and takes on the place and manner of the preceding stop. The change is confined to clusters and to Indo-Aryan, so it is rare as a cell.

examples.note: Sanskrit /gn/ became Pali geminate /gg/ by total progressive assimilation of the nasal to the preceding stop.
The Ashokan inscriptions write the geminate with a single letter; Gandhari has agi.
Also shows the Prakrit change of initial n to ṇ; the source of Hindi naṅgā and Romani nango.

sources: Wikipedia contributors (2026). Pali: Phonology, Assimilations. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pali
